title: Grover Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Grover wells have a 59 ft median depth, but records reach 900 ft. See yields, water levels, costs and risks before buying.
h1: What Grover, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land near Grover means checking more than whether a property has a well. Colorado DWR permit records show 356 wells within 5 miles, but only 115 are recorded as constructed. Depth, yield, water level and permitted use vary across the plains.

The local record points to generally shallow wells, strong reported yields and a mix of alluvial and sedimentary or fractured-bedrock water sources. Those results are useful for planning, but they do not guarantee what a new hole will produce on one particular lot.

sections.heading: Grover well depths range from shallow to very deep
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Grover is 59 feet. The middle half runs from 36 to 180 feet, meaning many wells are relatively shallow, while others require substantially more drilling. The record reaches 900 feet, and the 90th percentile is 400 feet.

Depth distribution gives a practical bidding range: 57% of wells are under 100 feet, 30% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 8% reach 300 to 600 feet, and 5% are 600 feet or deeper. A driller should still price the actual lot separately. Alluvium, plains sedimentary rock and fractured-bedrock conditions can change quickly over short distances.

sections.heading: Reported Grover yields are high, but the sample is limited
sections.html:
Only 46 wells report a pump yield, so the yield figures are a useful local signal rather than a promise for every parcel. Among those records, the median is 149.8 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 15.5 to 277.2 gallons per minute.

87% of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute, while 13% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. None of the reported wells are listed below 5 gallons per minute. Even a strong test result must be matched to the permitted use: an exempt household-use well is subject to Colorado’s 35-gpm pumping limit, and higher-demand uses may require different water rights or an augmentation plan.

sections.heading: Grover water levels look shallow, not clearly declining
sections.html:
There are 21 wells with a reported static water level. The median depth to water is 19 feet, and the middle half runs from 19 to 22 feet. That is a shallow measured water level compared with the range of total well depths.

The permit history does not establish a water-table trend. It shows permits by decade, not repeated water-level measurements from the same wells over time. Do not treat the clustered 19-to-22-foot readings as proof that water levels will remain unchanged. Ask for the well’s original report, recent pumping information and any available neighboring data before relying on it for a purchase or construction plan.

sections.heading: Recent permit activity matters when checking a Grover well
sections.html:
Grover-area records include permits from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2025. Permit counts were 15 in the 1950s, 14 in the 1960s, 24 in the 1970s, 11 in the 1980s, 12 in the 1990s, 60 in the 2000s, 102 in the 2010s and 35 in the 2020s.

The most frequent drillers in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 32 wells, Lesh Drilling Inc. (Lesh Jr., Ed) with 21, and Werner, Dallas D. with 12. These names help with record searches, but the permit, construction report and current pump condition matter more than the driller’s name alone.

sections.heading: A typical Grover well budget starts around the median depth
sections.html:
For alluvium and plains sedimentary rock near Grover, the drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the local median depth of 59 feet, that puts the drilled hole at about $2,100 to $3,200. That is not the complete project price.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at approximately $8,100 to $15,200 at that median depth. Deeper drilling, difficult access, casing and grout requirements, water-quality treatment, longer utility runs or an oversized system can move the bid higher. Request a written scope that separates drilling from pump equipment and site work so competing bids can be compared accurately.

sections.heading: PFAS and septic planning belong in the Grover inspection
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records within about 10 miles include 86 PFAS sampling or contamination sites. The same search shows 0 historic mine features and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. A mapped site does not by itself prove that a property’s well is contaminated, but it is a reason to test existing water and understand the local history.

Low-yield wells and dry holes remain possible even where nearby records look productive. Check casing, grout, pump setting, storage capacity and laboratory results. Septic placement also matters: keep the well, septic system, reserve area and building envelope coordinated with the county’s requirements. Confirm the permit allows the intended household, stock or irrigation use before designing the property around it.

sections.heading: Buy or build after verifying the exact lot
sections.html:
Start with the well permit and construction report for the property, then compare nearby records in Briggsdale, Raymer, Nunn, Pierce, Ault and Carr only as broader context. The local database shows 12% domestic or household wells, 29% stock wells, 28% irrigation wells and 17% monitoring wells, so nearby wells may not be comparable to a home supply.

Ask for a current flow or pump test, a recent water-quality test and a pump-system inspection. Confirm the well’s legal use with Colorado DWR, especially if the plan includes irrigation, livestock or additional structures. Before closing, price access, trenching, septic and electrical work together. A 59-foot median is encouraging for budgeting, but the range through 900 feet is the reason to investigate the actual parcel.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Grover, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Grover is 59 feet. The middle half runs from 36 to 180 feet. Most are under 100 feet, but the records also include wells reaching 900 feet, with 5% at 600 feet or deeper. A nearby well is a guide, not a guarantee for a new hole.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Grover?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 59-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,100 to $3,200. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $8,100 to $15,200. Deeper drilling, access problems and site-specific equipment can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Grover wells produce?
faq.a: Only 46 wells in the records report a pump yield. Their median reported yield is 149.8 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 15.5 to 277.2 gallons per minute. Reported production is strong overall, but those figures do not guarantee a new well’s result or establish the legal amount a household may pump.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Grover?
faq.a: The records do not establish that every Grover well is safe to drink. There are 86 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, so testing is important. Have the property’s water tested by a qualified laboratory, review the well construction and ask about nearby land uses before relying on it for a home.

faq.q: Are Grover well water levels going down?
faq.a: There are 21 static water-level reports. The median depth to water is 19 feet, and the middle half is 19 to 22 feet. Those readings suggest shallow water levels in the reported wells, but the permit data are not a repeated monitoring series. They cannot establish a long-term falling trend for Grover or for one specific property.
